<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README contents, “Chatlog” is a Go-based tool designed to extract, decrypt, and serve WeChat chat records through both a command-line interface (with a Terminal UI) and an HTTP API. It supports multiple platforms (Windows and macOS) and different WeChat versions (3.x and 4.0) while also integrating with MCP SSE for AI assistant tools.

Below is a detailed guide to creating an accurate, component-rich system design diagram tailored to this project:

1. Overall Architecture – Identify Major Components:
   • Command-Line Interface (CLI) & Terminal UI: Represented by the main executable (cmd/chatlog) and internal/ui packages (footer, help, infobar, menu, style). This component handles local user interactions.
   • HTTP API Service: The HTTP-related code inside internal/chatlog/http exposes REST endpoints (e.g., /api/v1/chatlog, /api/v1/contact, /api/v1/chatroom, /api/v1/session) plus the SSE endpoint for MCP.
   • Core Business Logic: Organized under internal/chatlog with supporting packages such as configuration (internal/chatlog/conf), context management (internal/chatlog/ctx), and application-level orchestration (app.go, manager.go).
   • Decryption & Key Extraction Modules: Encapsulated under internal/wechat (decrypt, key, process, manager) that handle reading memory/processes and decrypting WeChat data.
   • Data Access Layer: Constructed through internal/wechatdb (datasource and repository subpackages) which manage reading from the local WeChat database files.
   • MCP Protocol Integration: Under internal/mcp and parts of internal/chatlog/mcp that expose JSON-RPC, SSE, and other communication methods needed for interoperability with AI tools.
   • Utility and Support Libraries: Provided in pkg (appver, config, util such as for compression/zstd, dat2img, OS helpers) to support common operations across modules.
   • Error Handling: Modules under internal/errors coordinate robust error propagation across HTTP, OS, wechat, and MCP handling.

2. Mapping Relationships and Interactions:
   • The main executable (cmd/chatlog) initiates the system and routes to either CLI/Terminal UI or HTTP API interface.
   • For CLI/Terminal UI commands (e.g., key extraction, decrypt) the user input flows into the core logic modules which then call on the decryption (internal/wechat/decrypt and key) and database reading (internal/wechatdb) services.
   • When running as an HTTP service, incoming REST API requests are handled by the HTTP routing component (internal/chatlog/http/route.go) that delegates to service modules; these then query the local database repositories or perform decryption if needed.
   • The MCP component listens for SSE connections (via internal/mcp/sse.go) and coordinates responses using JSON-RPC style endpoints.
   • Utility packages in pkg support these functionalities by providing versioning, standardized configuration loading, and OS-specific operations.

3. Architectural Patterns and Principles:
   • Modular/Layered Design: Separate packages (cmd for CLI, internal for business logic, pkg for utilities) clearly separate concerns.
   • Clear Separation between Presentation (UI/HTTP), Business Logic, and Data Access.
   • Use of configuration and context packages for dependency injection and service orchestration.
   • Consistent error handling across different components using centralized internal/errors modules.

4. Diagramming Guidelines:
   • Use distinct blocks/boxes for each major component. For instance, represent “CLI/Terminal UI”, “HTTP API Service”, “Core Business Logic”, “WeChat Decryption Module”, “Database Access Layer”, “MCP Integration”, and “Utility/Error Handling” as separate nodes.
   • Draw directional arrows:
       - From the “User Input” to “CLI/Terminal UI” and “HTTP API Service”.
       - From these UI components towards the “Core Business Logic”.
       - Then, have arrows from the business logic to supporting components like “Decryption Module” (for reading keys and decrypting data) and “Database Access Layer” (for retrieving chat records).
       - Illustrate the flow from “Business Logic” to “MCP Integration” when SSE events or JSON-RPC communications are initiated.
   • Label each arrow to show the type of communication, such as “API Request”, “Decryption & Key Extraction call”, “Database Query”, etc.
   • Use color coding (or shapes) to mark different layers:
       - One color for presentation/UI layers.
       - Another color for business logic.
       - A different color for utility/support services like decryption and data access.
   • Ensure all external dependencies, such as OS-specific services (e.g., reading process memory on Windows or macOS, dependency on Xcode and lldb for macOS), are noted, perhaps as annotations around the “WeChat Decryption Module”.

5. Tailoring the Diagram for the Project Type:
   • As a tool that is both a command-line utility and an HTTP API server, the diagram should clearly split the “User Interface Layer” into two paths:
       - Local Terminal/CLI interactions.
       - Remote API interactions.
   • Emphasize the data flow from local WeChat database files (input source) towards the decryption and parsing modules and then to both output interfaces.
   • Highlight the integration with MCP SSE—depicting this as a side-channel that allows communication with external AI assistants or tools.
   • Consider adding annotations regarding cross-platform considerations (e.g., macOS-specific instructions for disabling SIP and using lldb, Windows-specific decryption paths).

6. Final Instructions for the Diagram:
   • Each component should have a clear and descriptive label (e.g., “HTTP API Router”, “Terminal UI”, “WeChat Decryption Service”).
   • Use directional arrows to show:
       - Data/input flow from the user interface to core processing.
       - How processed chat records go to database queries and/or API responses.
       - Interactions with error handling and utility modules.
   • Optionally include notes or legends in the diagram to explain color coding or shorthand labels.
   • Make sure the diagram is detailed, capturing even smaller subcomponents (like configuration, context management, etc.) if needed to understand the overall system – especially the paths that lead from command execution to decryption and database access.

Following these guidelines will help you produce a comprehensive and accurate system design diagram for the Chatlog project. The diagram will clearly illustrate how the CLI/HTTP layers interact with the core logic, supporting decryption and data access modules, plus how the MCP integration ties into the overall flow, providing clarity for both developers and stakeholders.
</explanation>
